石見神楽.tagline: Fast 'hacchoshi' rhythm and gorgeous costumes woven with gold and silver thread
石見神楽.intro: This is the traditional performing art that represents the Iwami region in western Shimane Prefecture. Its stories come from the myths of the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki (ancient Japanese chronicles). Dancers in gorgeous costumes decorated with gold and silver thread perform to music (hayashi) played on a large drum, a small drum, hand cymbals and a flute. On autumn festival nights, you can hear kagura music from shrines all around.
history: There are several theories about its origin, but it is said to have been performed already by the late Muromachi period. Its source is 'Omoto Kagura', which comes from the tradition of dengaku (field music and dance). It is thought that it took on its present, strongly theatrical form under the influence of Izumo-style kagura (Sada Shinno) and of Noh, Kyogen and Kabuki.

The big turning point came in the early Meiji era. Scholars of kokugaku (Japanese classical studies) revised kagura, and an order banned Shinto priests from dancing kagura. Because of this, local parishioners (people of the area) took over as dancers. This is called 'shinzoku kotai' (the handover from priests to lay people). Around the same time, many areas adopted the fast 'hacchoshi' (eight-beat) rhythm, and kagura is said to have become even more entertaining.

In 2019, Iwami Kagura and 15 component cultural properties were recognised as Japan Heritage. However, the Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan designation belongs to its source, 'Omoto Kagura' (designated in 1979). Iwami Kagura as a whole has not been designated by the national government, and many individual kagura are cultural properties of the prefecture or of cities, towns and villages.
features: By tempo, it falls into two main types: 'rokuchoshi' (six-beat rhythm) and 'hacchoshi'. Today the main style is hacchoshi, with its fast and intense beat.

The music uses a large drum, a small drum ('shime-daiko'), hand cymbals and a transverse flute. There is no written score. The large-drum player watches the dancers' movements and leads the whole ensemble.
The costumes are gorgeous, with plenty of gold and silver thread. The masks are papier-mache masks made from Sekishu washi, a Japanese paper that is a local speciality.

The serpent's body is light and folds like a bellows. It is made of Sekishu washi and bamboo. Originally the serpent was basically danced as a single serpent, but after the Second World War, performances with many serpents on stage became more common.

programs.name: Shiobarai (purification)
programs.text: A ritual dance that purifies and cleanses the kagura hall before the gods are welcomed. It is the most basic play.

programs.name: Orochi (the eight-headed serpent)
programs.text: Susanoo slays Yamata-no-Orochi, the eight-headed serpent. This is the star of Iwami Kagura, and it closes many performances.

programs.name: Iwato (the Heavenly Rock Cave)
programs.text: A play based on the myth of the Heavenly Rock Cave. After the cave is opened, the dancers take off their masks and perform a dance of joy.

programs.name: Ebisu
programs.text: A dance in which the god Ebisu fishes for a sea bream. In one scene, rice cakes and sweets are thrown to the audience, so it is popular with children.

programs.name: Kashima
programs.text: Based on the myth of 'kuni-yuzuri' (the handing over of the land), this is an unusual play in which gods grapple with each other.

viewing: Many performances are offerings at shrines or regular shows, and quite a few of them are free to watch.
If it is your first time, we recommend choosing a day when 'Orochi' is performed. You can enjoy a powerful stage.
The music is fast, so watch the large drum and the dancers' movements together to enjoy it even more.

高千穂神楽.tagline: Night kagura of 33 pieces, danced over a whole night
高千穂神楽.intro: This kagura is handed down in the town of Takachiho, Miyazaki Prefecture. At the kagura hall of Takachiho Shrine, four representative pieces out of the 33 are performed every night in about one hour. Every year from around November to February, all-night 'yokagura' (night kagura) is performed as an offering in about 20 communities in the town.
history: Takachiho Kagura is said to have its origin in the myth of Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto dancing in front of the Heavenly Rock Cave. In written records, the phrase 'gojinraku for seven days and seven nights' in a document from 1189 is regarded as the first appearance of a word for kagura. The word 'yokagura' appears in a document from 1754.
It is thought that until around the end of the Edo period, Shinto priests and shrine attendants performed it as an offering in shrine buildings and kagura halls.
In 1978 (Showa 53), it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
features: Every year from mid-November to early February, yokagura is held in about 20 communities in the town.
The venue is a 'kagura lodge' (kagura-yado), a private house in the community. Today, more and more communities use a community hall instead.
In principle there are 33 pieces. Their content differs from community to community, and they can be divided into five lineages.

On the afternoon of the first day, kagura is performed as an offering at the shrine of the local guardian god. Then the dancers enter the kagura lodge dancing, together with a portable shrine carrying the god's sacred object. This is called 'maikomi' (dancing in). After dancing through the night, the kagura ends with the sending-off of the gods the next morning.

programs.name: Goshintai
programs.text: A lively play in which Izanagi and Izanami dance the making of sake.

programs.name: Tajikarao
programs.text: A dance in which Tajikarao-no-Mikoto searches for and finds the rock door. In the next piece, 'Totori', he lifts the rock door and throws it away.

programs.name: Uzume
programs.text: A feminine dance representing Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto. The dancer turns slowly with small steps.

programs.name: Maibiraki
programs.text: The dancer dances holding, in both hands, the mirror that was inside the rock cave.

viewing: Night kagura in the communities goes on all night. Bring plenty of warm clothing.
The performance at the kagura hall of Takachiho Shrine, held every night (about 1 hour, 4 pieces), is easy to watch even for first-timers.
Spectators sometimes liven things up with 'kagura-seri' (lively calls from the audience). Please follow good manners so that you do not trouble the local people.

備中神楽.tagline: Myth plays performed in the 'kodono' (sacred hall)
備中神楽.intro: Bitchu Kagura, handed down in Okayama Prefecture, is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan. Old Japanese tales are staged as plays and danced powerfully. It is a Shinto ritual that prays for a rich harvest of the five grains.
history: In the Bitchu region of western Okayama Prefecture, 'Kojin Kagura', performed as an offering to the god Kojin, has been held since long ago. It centred on the dance of Sarutahiko and the sword dance, and only Shinto priests danced it.

In the Bunka and Bunsei eras of the Edo period (the early 1800s), [[西林国橋]], a Shinto priest and kokugaku (Japanese classical studies) scholar from Takahashi, is said to have added kagura of the Age of the Gods, based on myths, and completed its present form. It took in elements of Noh, Kyogen and Kabuki and became more entertaining as theatre. As a result, kagura performers (kagura-dayu) who were not Shinto priests also began to perform it as an offering.
In 1979 (Showa 54), it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
features: It combines the character of a Shinto ritual with the fun of theatre as a local folk performing art.
Matsuo Daimyojin plays the clown role called 'chari' (comic role). His banter with the drummer is unique and popular with audiences.
Today, kagura troupes in each district carry on the dances at local festivals and regular performances.

programs.name: Sarutahiko no Mai (the dance of Sarutahiko)
programs.text: The dance of Sarutahiko, who guides the way at the descent of the Heavenly Grandson. It preserves an old form of Kojin Kagura.

programs.name: Sword dance
programs.text: A brave dance performed with a sword in hand.

programs.name: Matsuo Daimyojin (Chari, the clown)
programs.text: A scene in which the clown banters with the drummer and makes the audience laugh.

viewing: Even if you do not know the story of the myths, the fun of the banter alone is enough to enjoy it.
Check the dates on the event information page before you go.

安芸高田神楽.intro: This kagura is handed down in Akitakata, Hiroshima Prefecture. For example, the kagura of Takamiya is known for its fast eight-beat tempo, and all the kagura troupes in the town are designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties of Hiroshima Prefecture. In the city there are places to watch kagura, such as the Kagura Dome at Kagura Monzen Tojimura.
history: Kagura in Akitakata is thought to be Izumo-style kagura that reached this area via Iwami Kagura in the Edo period. Along the way, it is said, it was also influenced by Hachiman-lineage kagura from Kyushu, Takachiho Kagura, Bitchu Kagura and the old farmers' beliefs of the Chugoku Mountains, and so took its present form.

The Kajiya Kagura Troupe is said to have begun in the mid-Edo period, when it learned kagura from Shinto priests of Asuna and [[上田村]] in Iwami (today's Onan, Shimane). It is called the founder of kagura culture in the city. The Yamane Kagura Troupe also says it began in 1790 (Kansei 2), when four people from the village learned kagura from a Shinto priest of Asuna and brought it home.

'Kyumai' refers to the dances and music of the 'Asuna-te' and 'Kajiya-te' styles, which already existed at the end of the Second World War and have been handed down to today. 'Shinmai', on the other hand, is kagura newly created after the war. Today it has spread widely, not only in Akitakata but throughout the Geihoku area.

In 1954 (Showa 29), four dances were designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties of Hiroshima Prefecture: 'Kamimukae' of the Ao Kagura Troupe, 'Kamioroshi' of the Kuwada Tenshi Kagura Troupe, 'Shoki' of the Kajiya Kagura Troupe and the sword dance ([[剣舞]]) of the Yamane Kagura Troupe. Shortly after the war, in 1949-52 (Showa 24-27), the [[神幸]] Kagura Troupe won more than 20 times at competitions in various places. This helped to spread the name of Midori kagura.
features: Akitakata is said to be the birthplace of shinmai. Shinmai shows off quick changes of costume and mask, fast fighting scenes, and flashy effects using dry ice and spider threads. Kyumai, based on the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, demands great skill to express the story through slow movements.

There are 22 kagura troupes active in the city. In this area, each local shrine has its own kagura troupe, and the local parishioners themselves dance, not Shinto priests. Members carry on kagura alongside their work or studies.
The music is played on a large drum, a small drum, hand cymbals and a flute. The large drum leads the rhythm of the whole ensemble, and this part is often taken by the troupe leader.

The demon role is said to be the hardest to dance. Another highlight is the 'ureshi-mai' (dance of joy), danced by a god after winning a fight. In some plays, a role called 'chari' also appears: a performer who stands on stage alone and makes the audience laugh.

programs.name: Takiyasha-hime (Princess Takiyasha)
programs.text: Princess Satsuki, daughter of Taira no Masakado, receives magic powers from the god of Kibune to avenge her father's bitter death. She renames herself Takiyasha-hime and plots a rebellion. The highlight is the battle of yin-yang magic against her sorcery, fought by the onmyoji (yin-yang master) Oya no Chujo Mitsukuni and others.

programs.name: Momijigari (the autumn-leaf outing)
programs.text: Taira no Koremochi and his party lose their way on Mount Togakushi in Shinshu. They are invited to a banquet of beautiful women and fall under the spell of a demon woman. Hachiman Daibosatsu appears in Koremochi's dream and gives him a divine sword, and with it he defeats the demon woman.

programs.name: Tsuchigumo (the earth spider)
programs.text: The spirit of an earth spider living on Mount Katsuragi in Yamato Province disguises itself as a maid of Minamoto no Raiko and poisons him. Raiko's four great retainers suffer from the spider's magic of spitting threads, but they defeat it with the sword 'Kumokirimaru'.

programs.name: Yamata-no-Orochi (the eight-headed serpent)
programs.text: In Izumo, an old couple has lost one daughter after another to the serpent. Susanoo appears, makes the serpent drunk with poisoned sake and slays it. A sword comes out of the serpent's belly. It is named Ame-no-Murakumo-no-Tsurugi and offered to Amaterasu.

programs.name: Iwato-mai (the Rock Cave dance)
programs.text: In the Haji kagura handed down by the Yachiyo Kagura Troupe, the final duet of Iwato-mai is a dance with a shimenawa (sacred straw rope), and the dancers then hang the rope over the entrance of the Rock Cave. This follows the old story that the cave was closed so that Amaterasu would never go back inside.

viewing: There are two kinds of kagura: 'hono kagura', performed as an offering at shrine festivals, and 'hall kagura', which you pay to watch. At hall kagura, an MC often introduces the story, or sheets with the plot are handed out, so first-timers can easily follow the story.

At Kagura Monzen Tojimura, regular performances are held at the Kagura Dome and at Kamukura-za. The plays are announced about one week in advance. One play lasts about 40 minutes on average (about 30 minutes for short ones, about 90 minutes for long ones).

Every year on a Saturday in late September, the 'Midori Kagura Showcase' is held, with all 13 kagura troupes of Midori town performing. There is also the 'Takamiya Kagura Festival' of Takamiya kagura, which is known for its fast eight-beat tempo.
Kagura audiences are relaxed. You may eat and drink while watching, or call out to the performers. However, please avoid anything that bothers the people around you.

広島神楽.tagline: 'Hayagawari', where costumes change in an instant
広島神楽.intro: Kagura in Hiroshima Prefecture falls broadly into these lineages: Geihoku Kagura, Aki Juni Jingi, the kagura of the Geiyo Islands, Hiba Kojin Kagura and Bingo Kagura. In the prefecture there are regular performances every Wednesday, and kagura festivals and kagura competitions are held in many places.
history: Kagura in Hiroshima Prefecture differs greatly in character depending on the lineage. 'Geihoku Kagura', handed down in the Geihoku area in the west of the prefecture, such as Kitahiroshima and Akitakata, is said to have its source in Iwami Kagura of Shimane Prefecture.

Geihoku Kagura has 'kyumai' (old-style dances), handed down from before the Second World War, and 'shinmai' (new-style dances), born after the war. Shinmai is said to have been created while kagura was restricted after the war, with less Shinto character and more entertainment.

On the other hand, 'Juni Jingi Kagura' is handed down along the coast of the Seto Inland Sea (in Hiroshima, Hatsukaichi, Otake and other cities). It has a strong ritual character, and its dances are basically slow and calm.
features: Kyumai is also called 'hacchoshi' (fast eight-beat rhythm). It is danced with showy movements to fast music.
Shinmai developed by taking in new storylines and unique staging. It has highlights such as 'hayagawari' (quick change), where a costume changes in an instant.
Juni Jingi Kagura has slow, calm dances and keeps a strong ritual character.

programs.name: Orochi (the eight-headed serpent)
programs.text: Susanoo slays Yamata-no-Orochi. This is a standard kagura play.

programs.name: Takiyasha-hime (Princess Takiyasha)
programs.text: A play with a strong story. The quick costume changes are among its highlights.

viewing: There are everyday chances to watch kagura, such as the regular performance every Wednesday.
If you compare kyumai (slow and old-fashioned) with shinmai (showy, with a focus on staging), you can see the differences clearly.
At kagura festivals and competitions, you can enjoy the dances of many kagura troupes in one day.

庄内神楽.tagline: Kagura with a record of an offering performance in 1778
庄内神楽.intro: This kagura is handed down in Shonai, Yufu City, Oita Prefecture. It is danced bravely and colourfully to lively drums and flutes at a fast tempo. From May to October there are regular performances at the kagura hall of Shonai General Sports Park, and the Shonai Kagura Festival is held in autumn.
history: There is a record that shrine families performed kagura as an offering in 1778 (An'ei 7). It is said to have taken its present form in the early Meiji era.

The Shonai-district lineage began in the early Meiji era, when Sato Kikutaro of [[高津]] was taught Inuyama Kagura and set up a kagura troupe ('kagura-za'). The Asono-district lineage has its origin in [[深山流]] kagura of Asaji town.
In 2007 (Heisei 19), it was designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Yufu City, and in 2008 it was also recognised as an 'Oita Heritage'.
features: The instruments are a large drum, a small drum, a transverse flute and small cymbals ('dobyoshi'). It is danced bravely and colourfully to lively music.
Thirteen groups are active: 12 kagura troupes plus a volunteers' group.
In 'Orochi Taiji' by the Onoya Kagura-za, four serpents appear, the largest number in Shonai Kagura.

programs.name: Goho Reishi (greeting the five directions)
programs.text: The first dance, which welcomes the gods of the five directions and purifies the place.

programs.name: Orochi Taiji (slaying the serpent)
programs.text: An impressive play in which the serpent appears.

programs.name: Tobiraki (opening the rock door)
programs.text: A play based on the myth of opening the Heavenly Rock Cave.

viewing: From May to October, on the third Saturday of the month, the kagura troupes take turns giving regular performances at the kagura hall of Shonai General Sports Park.
At the 'Shonai Kagura Festival' in autumn, you can see the dances of several kagura troupes.

御嶽神楽.tagline: Brave, powerful dances with vigorous movements
御嶽神楽.intro: This kagura is handed down in southern Oita Prefecture and is an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan (designated in 2007). It preserves 33 plays based on myths and is known for brave dances with vigorous movements. The first play, [[五方礼始]], purifies the place, and the last one is always [[大神]], which celebrates peace throughout the land. There is also a scene in which the dancers and the audience pull against each other on a branch of sakaki (a sacred evergreen tree).
history: This kagura is handed down in Kiyokawa, Bungo-ono City, Oita Prefecture, and is said to be the origin of Ontake-ryu kagura. According to tradition, it began in 1449 (Hotoku 1), when kagura was performed as an offering to celebrate the founding of Ontake Shrine.

In the mid-Edo period, [[加藤長古]] is said to have taken in the forms of Izumo Kagura and completed its present form. After the Second World War, there was a time when depopulation put its survival at risk, but the whole village worked to preserve it, and it became active again.
In 2007, it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
features: There are 33 plays in all. Each one is basically in three parts: 'entrance', 'main dance' and 'exit'.
It is danced bravely to music played on a large drum, a small drum ('shime-daiko'), a small gong and a transverse flute.
It is the custom to purify the place first with [[五方礼始]].

programs.name: Goho Reishi (greeting the five directions)
programs.text: The first dance, in which the gods of the five directions purify the place.

programs.name: Ame-no-Nuboko (the heavenly spear)
programs.text: A play showing the myth of the birth of the land.

programs.name: Tenson Korin (the descent of the Heavenly Grandson)
programs.text: It shows the scene in which Ninigi-no-Mikoto descends to earth.

programs.name: Iwato-biraki (opening the Rock Cave)
programs.text: A dance of the myth in which Amaterasu hides in the Rock Cave.

viewing: Every year on the first Sunday of April, the 'Ontake-ryu Kagura Taikai' (kagura gathering) is held at the park [[能場公園]] in Kiyokawa. You can see Ontake-ryu kagura from inside and outside the prefecture.

銀鏡神楽.tagline: Danced through the night at the grand festival of Shiromi Shrine
銀鏡神楽.intro: This kagura is handed down at Shiromi Shrine in Saito City, Miyazaki Prefecture. Every year the grand festival runs from 12 to 16 December. During it, from the night of the 14th into the next day, the kagura pieces from 'Shiki 1' to 'Shiki 33' are performed all night as an offering. The kagura ends with 'Shishitogiri' and 'Kami-okuri' (sending off the gods), danced on the afternoon of the 15th.
history: This kagura is performed as an offering every December at the grand festival of Shiromi Shrine in Saito City, Miyazaki Prefecture. The official name used by the Agency for Cultural Affairs is 'Mera no Kagura', which groups together the kagura of Saito City, Kijo town and Nishimera village. It was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan in 1977 (Showa 52) under the name 'Mera Kagura', and the name was changed to the present one in 2023.
It is described as the first kagura in Miyazaki Prefecture to be designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
features: The heart of the grand festival, which runs from 12 to 16 December, is the all-night kagura from the night of the 14th into the 15th.
Wearing various masks, the dancers perform 33 kagura pieces through the night.
The kagura ends with 'Shishitogiri' and 'Kami-okuri' on the afternoon of the 15th.

programs.name: Shishitogiri
programs.text: The closing play of the grand festival, danced on the afternoon of the 15th.

programs.name: Kami-okuri (sending off the gods)
programs.text: A dance at the end of the kagura that sends the gods on their way.

viewing: It gets very cold during the all-night kagura. Bring warm clothing and a mat to sit on.
The dates may change from year to year. Check the latest information with the Saito City Tourism Association or other sources.

土佐の神楽.tagline: Kagura carried on at shrines' autumn festivals
土佐の神楽.intro: This kagura is performed as an offering at the autumn festivals of shrines in the mountain areas of Kochi Prefecture. Ikegawa Kagura, Nanokawa Iwato Kagura and Nagafuchi Kagura (Iwahara and Nagafuchi Kagura) were designated Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties of Japan in 1980. Tsunoyama Koshiki Kagura is also designated as part of 'Tosa no Kagura' (the kagura of Tosa).
history: 'Tosa no Kagura' is a collective name for the kagura handed down along the Shikoku Mountains in Kochi Prefecture. It consists of dances performed holding bells or sakaki branches, and theatrical dances based on the myths of the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki. By lineage, it is classed as Izumo Kagura.

On 28 January 1980 (Showa 55), it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan as 'Tosa no Kagura'. The groups that protect it include the Tsunoyama Kagura preservation societies of Yusuhara town and Tsuno town (formerly Higashitsuno village) and the Ikegawa Kagura Preservation Society.

Tsunoyama Kagura has been handed down since its preservation society was founded in 1948. On the other hand, in some districts the tradition has died out because of population decline and a lack of successors.
features: Special effort goes into the sword dances [[二天]] and [[三刄の舞]], and into acrobatic dances using trays and halberds.
Other distinctive plays include 'Shiten Kijin' and 'Akuma-barai'. In them, a person in a demon mask makes mischief, loses an argument, leaves treasures behind and runs away.
In some areas, 'saimon kagura', centred on prayer rituals, still survives. Because it keeps elements of spoken storytelling, it is said to preserve an older form.

programs.name: Sword dances
programs.text: A dance with swords, full of tension.

programs.name: Bon (Zen) no Mai / Naginata no Mai (tray dance and halberd dance)
programs.text: An acrobatic dance handling trays and halberds.

programs.name: Shiten Kijin / Akuma-barai (driving out demons)
programs.text: A play with a story, in which a demon loses an argument and runs away.

viewing: Most performances are offerings at shrine autumn festivals. Many venues are in the mountains, so travelling by car is the usual way to get there.
Check the dates and venues on the event information page before you go.

伊勢大神楽.intro: A traditional performing art handed down in Tayu, Kuwana, Mie Prefecture. Since the Edo period, its performers are said to have travelled from place to place, handing out charms from Ise Grand Shrine. It has two parts: lion dances that drive away misfortune, and 'hokagei' (acrobatic feats), which preserves the street performance of the early modern era. In 1981 it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
history: Ise Daikagura is the art of kagura performers who travel from place to place performing lion dances. There are several theories about its origin, but it is said to have a history of 450-600 years. Its home base is Masuda Shrine in Tayu, Kuwana, Mie Prefecture.

In the Edo period, the shogunate and Ise Grand Shrine recognised the performers as having the status of Shinto priests. They travelled the provinces and also had ties with feudal lords in many regions. At its peak there were 12 head families (shrine families), but only 5 head families are active today.
It became a cultural property of Mie Prefecture in 1954. In 1981 (Showa 56) it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
features: The performers visit homes and dance the lion dance as a prayer, for example to purify the kitchen hearth. In the past they visited Ise Grand Shrine on behalf of others, and they still hand out Ise Daikagura charms today.
In certain villages, they perform the highly entertaining 'somai' (full performance) at shrines and other places.
Plays with 'kyoku' in their names are hokagei (acrobatics). Between them comes 'manzai', a comic performance by a clown and an acrobat.

programs.name: Suzu no Mai, Shiho no Mai, Tobi no Mai (bell, four-directions and leaping dances)
programs.text: Lion dance plays. The dancer performs holding the lion head.

programs.name: Ayatori no Kyoku, Mizu no Kyoku, Sara no Kyoku (acrobatic feats)
programs.text: Hokagei plays. Their acrobatics thrill the audience.

programs.name: Kasa no Kyoku, Temari no Kyoku (umbrella and ball feats)
programs.text: Superb acrobatic feats using props.

viewing: At Masuda Shrine, the home base, all the head families gather every year on 24 December to perform the somai as an offering.
You can also see it at local events, such as the festival at Daifukudenji Temple on 2 April and the somai at Kuwana Sosha Shrine.

花祭.tagline: A festival of demons and hot-water rites, danced through the night
花祭.intro: A traditional performing art of Okumikawa (Toei, Toyone and other areas) in Aichi Prefecture, said to have continued for over 700 years. It is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan. From November to January, each village holds it through the night, with dances of gods and demons and 'yudate' (hot-water rites).
history: Hana Matsuri is a winter festival of yudate rites and dances, held in the villages of Okumikawa. It is said to be a traditional performing art that has continued for over 700 years, and it is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
The Hana Matsuri of Toei is divided into three lineages: Furikusa, Onyu and Okochi. Each village holds a slightly different festival.
features: Besides dances in masks of gods and demons, there is yudate, which uses hot water from a cauldron. In one scene, a demon uses a broad axe to toss up the pile of the bonfire.

The dance floor is decorated with things such as the 'yubuta' (literally 'hot-water lid'), made of paper in five colours. In some districts there is a custom at dawn of poking the 'hachi no su' (beehive) on the ceiling and picking up what falls out.

Spectators also stay all night and help liven up the festival. If you take an offering of money to the 'kaisho' (festival office) at the venue, you receive a gift in return that is unique to that place.

programs.name: Sakaki-oni (the sakaki-tree demon)
programs.text: One of the main demons. Some districts regard it as the god Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto.

programs.name: Yubayashi (the hot-water rite)
programs.text: The yudate scene, using the hot water in the cauldron.

programs.name: Iwato-biraki (opening the Heavenly Rock Cave)
programs.text: A dance based on the old story of Amaterasu hiding in the Heavenly Rock Cave.

viewing: The festival goes on all night, so warm clothing is essential. Public transport is limited in the area, so decide in advance how you will get home.
Venues are places such as village community halls, and parking space is limited. Share cars where you can.
You can check the dates for each district with the Education Section of Toei Town Office (0536-76-0509).

保呂羽山の霜月神楽.tagline: A hot-water kagura of 33 rites, performed through the night
保呂羽山の霜月神楽.intro: A nationally designated 'yudate kagura' (hot-water kagura). It is performed as an offering through the night from 7 to 8 November every year at the 'satomiya' (village shrine) of Haushiwake Shrine in Omori, Yokote, Akita Prefecture. Shrine maidens dance, and the climax comes when hot water from the cauldron before the altar is sprinkled over worshippers with bamboo grass.
history: It is regarded as a kagura of the Ise lineage that keeps the form of 'yoriai kagura', in which Shinto priests from nearby villages gather to perform. It is also said to pass down the original form of the shrine maiden to the present day.
It is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
features: Thirty-three rites are performed through the night.

Shrine maidens dance the 'Tendo-mai' and the 'Horowasan-mai'. Partway through there is a scene in which an oracle (the words of the gods) is delivered. In the middle of the night, the 'Yama-no-Kami-mai' and the [[神入舞]] are danced.
The climax is when hot water from the cauldron before the altar is sprinkled over worshippers with bamboo grass.

programs.name: Tendo-mai, Horowasan-mai (the shrine maidens' dances)
programs.text: The basic dances, performed by shrine maidens.

programs.name: Yama-no-Kami-mai and the god-entry dance
programs.text: Plays danced in the middle of the night.

viewing: Watching is free, but it is usual to give an offering of money ('hatsuhoryo') wrapped in paper.
There is parking for 30 cars. It is about 35 minutes by car from JR Omagari Station. Nights get very cold, so come prepared with warm clothing.

春日若宮おん祭.tagline: Performing arts offered into the night at Kasuga Taisha Shrine in December
春日若宮おん祭.intro: The festival of Wakamiya, a subsidiary shrine of Kasuga Taisha Shrine in Nara City, held every December. In the 'Owatari-shiki' on 17 December, groups of performers walk in procession to worship. At the 'Otabisho-sai', kagura by shrine maidens, 'dengaku' (field music and dance), 'bugaku' (court dance) and more are performed as offerings into the night.
history: The Owatari-shiki is a Shinto rite in which performing groups and others taking part in the festival form a procession and go to the 'otabisho' (the temporary shrine) of the Wakamiya deity.
features: At the Otabisho-sai, kagura by shrine maidens, dengaku, bugaku and more are performed as offerings on a turf stage into the night.
Some rites are held in the middle of the night.

programs.name: Kagura (Shaden Kagura, the shrine's own kagura)
programs.text: It centres on the 'yaotome-mai' (dance of the eight maidens) by the shrine maidens of Kasuga Taisha Shrine, called 'mikanko'. Its origin is said to go back to the early Heian period. Six pieces are danced, including dances for two, one, six and four dancers. The costumes are also the most formal ones used at Kasuga Taisha Shrine.

programs.name: Azuma Asobi (dances of the east)
programs.text: It is regarded as a dance of the eastern provinces. It comes from an old story that a heavenly maiden came down to the shore of Suruga and danced. After the bonfires are lit, four children wearing swords dance the 'Suruga-mai' and the 'Motomego-mai'. It is said to be rare for children to dance it.

programs.name: Dengaku (field music and dance)
programs.text: A performing art that has been offered since the On-matsuri began. The performers present a large ritual wand in five colours before the deity. After the music, they show the acrobatic feats 'Katanadama' (sword juggling) and 'Takaashi' (stilt), and finally perform a short Noh play.

programs.name: Seinoo
programs.text: It is thought to be a performing art of the Hachiman deity tradition, linked to an old story about Empress Jingu. Six performers in white ritual robes hang white cloths below their eyes. To the small hand drum and the flute, they move forward and back while covering their faces with their sleeves. It is a simple, mysterious dance.

programs.name: Sarugaku (Kagura-shiki)
programs.text: The 'Kagura-shiki', a shortened form of the Noh play 'Okina', is performed. Okina and Sanbaso dance without masks, in white ritual robes. This special Okina for the otabisho of the On-matsuri was established at the beginning of the Meiji era.

programs.name: Bugaku (court dance)
programs.text: Dances that came from the Asian continent and were perfected in Japan. Left dances in reddish costumes and right dances in greenish costumes are paired, and 10 pieces are danced in 5 pairs. For 'Ranryo-o' and 'Nasori', the dance of the side that won the horse race at the Owatari-shiki is performed first.

viewing: There are 'sajiki' (reserved seats) where you can watch the Owatari-shiki sitting down. Bookings are taken from 20 October to 14 December through 'NARA Time', Nara City's booking site for sightseeing experiences, or by phone.
If the Owatari-shiki is cancelled because of the weather, some of the reserved seats are cancelled too. There are no refunds.

遠山の霜月祭.tagline: A kagura of masks and hot-water rites, with boiling water splashed about
遠山の霜月祭.intro: A 'yudate kagura' (hot-water kagura) held every December in Tohyama-go (Kamimura and Minami-Shinano) in Iida, Nagano Prefecture. Each shrine holds it on a different day. Water is boiled in a cauldron to welcome the gods, and masked gods dance. It goes on through the night, and it is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
history: The leading theory on its origin is that it was a ritual of the estates, brought in during the Kamakura period when the Toyama valley was an estate of Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine. The procession of the masks is thought to have been added in the Edo period.
In 1973 it was selected by the national government as an intangible folk cultural property. On 3 February 1979 (Showa 54) it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
features: Broadly, it falls into four types: Kamimachi, Shimoguri, Kizawa and Wada. They differ in the number of cauldrons, the number of yudate rites, the number of masks, and the time when the masks appear.
The number of masks is 15-17 for the Kamimachi type, 39 for Shimoguri, 25-37 for Kizawa and 41 for Wada (according to Iida City materials).
The festival begins with the preparations and the eve festival, and runs until the clearing-up, called [[三日・算日]]. In all, it lasts four days and two nights.

programs.name: Yudate (hot-water rite)
programs.text: A rite in which water is boiled in a cauldron to welcome the gods.

programs.name: The masks appear (Men no Tojo)
programs.text: A wild scene in which masked gods appear and splash boiling water.

viewing: The festival lasts a whole day and night. Bring food that is easy to eat, and something to keep your feet warm.
As a rule, the public may go only as far as the dance hall where the cauldron is. Watch from a place where you will not get in the way.
The dates are only a guide and may move earlier or later. Before you go, check with the Iida City or Tohyama-go offices.

秩父神楽.tagline: The kagura of Chichibu Shrine, based on classical myths
秩父神楽.intro: A kagura handed down at Chichibu Shrine in Chichibu, Saitama Prefecture. It is also called 'Jindai Kagura' (kagura of the age of the gods). Its special feature is that its stories come from classical myths, such as the myths of Takamagahara (the plain of heaven) and of Izumo. It is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
history: Until the early Meiji era, it was 'shake kagura', handed down by the families of the priests who served Chichibu Shrine. There were originally 75 pieces, but today they have been brought together into 35 plays. It nearly died out several times along the way, but it has been passed down to the present.
features: Unlike typical 'sato kagura' (village kagura), it takes its themes from classical myths, such as the myths of Takamagahara and of Izumo.

It is performed as an offering in the kagura hall on set days several times a year, such as the first kagura of the year (2 January), the Setsubun festival for driving out demons (3 February) and the annual festival (2 and 3 December).

programs.name: No. 7: Ama-no-Iwato-biraki (opening the Heavenly Rock Cave)
programs.text: A signature play of Chichibu Shrine. It centres on Yagokoro-Omoikane-no-Mikoto, who is also enshrined at the shrine, and shows the scene in which Amaterasu, hidden in the Heavenly Rock Cave, is comforted. It is performed at every offering, and it is a large play that needs 11 or more kagura performers.

programs.name: No. 18: Daisangu (visiting the shrine on behalf of others)
programs.text: A kagura danced 'sumen' (without a mask), which is unusual among the plays of Chichibu Shrine. At the Chichibu Night Festival on 3 December, it is performed before the deity at the 'saijo-sai' rite held at night at the otabisho (the deity's temporary shrine).

programs.name: No. 35: Orochi Taiji (slaying the eight-headed serpent)
programs.text: The last of the 35 plays. It was also performed in the kagura offering at the 2024 Chichibu Night Festival.

viewing: The December annual festival falls at the same time as the Chichibu Night Festival, and the whole town gets very crowded. Allow plenty of time.
Check the kagura times with Chichibu Shrine before you go.

鷲宮催馬楽神楽.tagline: Kagura regarded as the source of Edo kagura in the Kanto region
鷲宮催馬楽神楽.intro: A kagura handed down at Washinomiya Shrine in Kuki, Saitama Prefecture. It is regarded as the source of Edo kagura in the Kanto region. Its special feature is that its kagura songs take in 'saibara', songs of gagaku (court music). It is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
history: It was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan on 4 May 1976 (Showa 51). The kagura hall of Washinomiya Shrine, the stage where it is performed, was built in 1821 (Bunsei 4).
features: Its special feature is that its kagura songs take in saibara from gagaku.
It is performed six times a year in the kagura hall of Washinomiya Shrine: on 1 January, 14 February, 10 April, 31 July, 10 October, and the first Day of the Rooster in December.

programs.name: No. 1: Amateru Kuniteru Futonorito Shinei no Mai (the opening prayer)
programs.text: A solo dance without a mask. The dancer first holds a fan, then changes to a paper wand and a bell. Because this play reads out a prayer for the kagura that follows to go safely, it is placed first of the 12 pieces.

programs.name: No. 4: Korin Misaki Sarutahiko Uzume no Mai (Sarutahiko and Uzume)
programs.text: Two dancers perform: one in a tengu (goblin) mask carrying a spear, and one in the mask of Uzume carrying a red paper wand. Based on the myth of the descent of the heavenly grandson, it is a festive play that prays for rich harvests of the five grains and peace in the land. It is said that it was also danced to pray for safe childbirth.

programs.name: No. 5: Iwato Shokai Shojin Daiki no Mai (the gods rejoice as the cave opens)
programs.text: A dance by three performers: two shrine maidens without masks and one in an old man's mask. Based on the myth of the Heavenly Rock Cave, it is said to show people rejoicing that the light has returned.

programs.name: No. 6: Yashima Kigen Ukihashi Waza no Mai (the birth of the land)
programs.text: A play of the 'kuniumi' (birth of the land) myth, danced by two performers: Izanagi holding a sun emblem and Izanami holding a moon emblem. It is also said to be a dance that prays for many descendants and good fortune.

programs.name: No. 11: Chinakujin Hakkyu Utsubo no Mai (subduing evil gods with bow and quiver)
programs.text: Two dancers in the masks of the Minister of the Right and the Minister of the Left dance boldly with bows and arrows. It is a kagura to calm demons and drive away curses, and it is said that it was also performed when epidemics spread.

programs.name: Hakagura (the interlude kagura)
programs.text: Between plays, a single shrine maiden without a mask dances holding a paper wand and a bell. There is no fixed tune. She dances to suit the next play, as if purifying the stage from one end to the other.

viewing: The performance days are the same every year, but the start time is not fixed exactly and varies from day to day. According to the published guidance, it often starts at around 11 a.m. and ends at around 3 p.m. Only on 1 January is it also performed from around midnight.
The plays are not decided in advance, so you will not know them until the day. It is held together with the shrine's festivals, and anyone may watch.
Washinomiya Shrine is about a 10-minute walk from Washinomiya Station on the Tobu Isesaki Line. The shrine has a car park.

相模里神楽.area: Atsugi and other areas, Kanagawa Prefecture
相模里神楽.tagline: A silent kagura that acts out myths in masks
相模里神楽.intro: A 'sato kagura' (village kagura) handed down in Kanagawa Prefecture. It is a silent drama, performed in masks, based on myths from the 'Kojiki', the 'Nihon Shoki' and other sources. It is also called 'Jindai Kagura'. Besides offerings at shrines, it is also staged at community centres and halls.
history: The origins of Jindai Kagura are not clear. It is said that in the mid-Edo period the Mibu Kyogen of Kyoto was performed in Edo, developed there, and then spread to the Sagami region.

In Aiko, Atsugi, there were three kagura head families. Their kagura was called 'Aiko Kagura' and was widely performed as a Shinto rite offered at shrines. However, it declined after the Meiji Restoration.

In 1912 (Meiji 45), a relative of one of the three head families took over Aiko Kagura as 'Sagami Sato Kagura'. This is today's Sagami Sato Kagura Kakizawa Shachu (kagura troupe). On 1 July 1971 (Showa 46) it was designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Atsugi City. The current head of the family is the third generation.
features: There are no spoken lines. The story moves forward through the gestures of the masked dancers and the music (hayashi).
The Sagami Sato Kagura Kakizawa Shachu of Atsugi also performs at community centres in the city, as part of the city's performances to promote local folk arts.

programs.name: Kumaso Seibatsu (the conquest of the Kumaso)
programs.text: Yamato-Oguna, a 16-year-old boy, puts on a robe given to him by his aunt Yamato-hime and disguises himself as a woman. He slips into a banquet of the Kumaso brothers and kills them both. At the end, the younger brother gives him his name, and Yamato Takeru is born.

programs.name: Tenson Korin (the descent of the heavenly grandson)
programs.text: Ninigi, the grandson of Amaterasu, comes down to earth with Uzume, goddess of the performing arts, and lands safely, guided by Sarutahiko. Near the end, Sarutahiko performs the 'Kumokiri' (cloud cutting), clearing the way with a spear.

programs.name: Hohi no Joshi (Hohi the envoy)
programs.text: A scene from the story of the handing over of the land. Ame-no-Hohi comes down to earth on Amaterasu's orders, but through a trick by Okuninushi he is made to drink sake. He gets drunk, fails in his mission and sinks into gloom. It is one of the plays the Kakizawa Shachu is best at.

programs.name: Yakumo Shinei (Yamata-no-Orochi Taiji: slaying the eight-headed serpent)
programs.text: Susanoo meets Kushinada-hime and an old couple who are weeping because the serpent has taken their daughters. He gets Orochi drunk on strong sake, then fights and slays it. The sword that comes out of Orochi's tail later becomes the sword Ame-no-Murakumo-no-Tsurugi.

programs.name: Sakaki no Mai (Shinzen-mai, dance before the gods)
programs.text: 'Shinzen-mai' are the basic dances offered at shrine festivals, and the foundation of all kagura dances. The Kakizawa Shachu has seven shinzen-mai. This dance is performed holding 'sakaki' branches, in which gods are said to dwell, and it stands for purification.

viewing: Some performances at community centres are short, about 30 minutes. Plays and times may change, so check before you go.

鎌倉神楽.area: Kamakura, Fujisawa and other areas, Kanagawa Prefecture
鎌倉神楽.tagline: A hot-water kagura danced by Shinto priests
鎌倉神楽.intro: A kagura with 'yudate' (hot-water rites), handed down at shrines in Kamakura and Fujisawa, Kanagawa Prefecture. It is also called 'Yubana Kagura' and is performed as an offering by Shinto priests alone. They stir the hot water in a large cauldron, and sprinkle hot water from dipped bamboo grass over the people attending.
history: Kamakura Kagura is a type of yudate kagura. It is said to have come about 800 years ago from Iwashimizu Hachimangu Shrine in Kyoto to Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine in Kamakura. Kotai Jingu Shrine in Fujisawa describes it as a kagura passed down since the beginning of the Kamakura period by the 'kagura-o' (kagura men) of Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine.

In Kanagawa Prefecture, this kagura is carried on by shrines descended from the families that served as kagura-o at Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine, known as the 'Shokusho Hakke' (eight families of office). There are two lineages, Sano and Yoshida. Shirahata Shrine in Fujisawa carries on the Yoshida lineage.

Its name differs from place to place. In Fujisawa it has been called 'Yudate Kagura' or 'Yubana Kagura', and among fishermen 'Shio Kagura' (tide kagura). According to Shirahata Shrine, most of the yudate kagura performed in Fujisawa, Kamakura and Hayama is the same kagura.

In Kamakura it is carried on by the Shinto priests of the Kamakura Kagura Preservation Society, and it is a designated cultural property of Kamakura City. The yudate kagura of Fujisawa was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Fujisawa City on 1 March 1996 (Heisei 8).
features: The plays include 'Hano' and 'Gohei Maneki', danced to flute, 'shime-daiko' drum and 'odo' drum; 'Kakiyu', in which boiling water is stirred with a 'gohei' (ritual paper wand); and 'Sasa-mai', in which hot water is sprinkled from dipped bamboo grass.
At the autumn festival of Shirahata Shrine in Fujisawa, 12 pieces are performed as offerings. During the sword dance and 'Modoki', sweets and rice cakes are scattered to the people attending.

programs.name: Hano (the first dance)
programs.text: A dance that purifies the kagura space. The dancer places washed rice on a fan and, holding a bell, offers the rice to the four directions. At Shirahata Shrine it is danced by the chief priest.

programs.name: Gohei Maneki (inviting the gods)
programs.text: A dance that invites the three gods welcomed to the kagura: the local guardian god, the god of fire and the god of water. After the dance there is a rite in which the people attending receive the spirit of the gods.

programs.name: Kakiyu (stirring the hot water)
programs.text: The boiling water in the large cauldron is stirred with a gohei, sending drops of hot water flying. It is the dance that symbolises yudate kagura. In the old days, the way the water boiled was used to tell whether the year would be good or bad.

programs.name: Yugura, Sasa no Mai (bamboo grass dance)
programs.text: Two dancers shake bamboo grass dipped in boiling water, scattering spray over the heads of the people attending. Being splashed by this spray is said to keep away misfortune and illness.

programs.name: Iharai (purifying with arrows)
programs.text: Arrows are shot to the four corners to drive away evil spirits, and finally an arrow is shot towards the altar. Receiving one of the arrows is said to bring good fortune and good health.

programs.name: Sword dance and Modoki (comic imitation)
programs.text: A tengu (goblin) in a red mask purifies evil with a sword and prays for good harvests, big catches of fish and peace in the land. Partway through, a mountain god in a black mask appears and clowns around, imitating the tengu. The kagura ends with everyone relaxed and laughing.

viewing: In the plays where hot water is sprinkled, you may get splashed.
The content may change because of rain or for other reasons.

海南神社面神楽.tagline: Kainan Shrine's kagura, danced in masks
海南神社面神楽.intro: This kagura is handed down at Kainan Shrine in Misaki, Miura, Kanagawa Prefecture. It is also called 'Jindai Kagura' (kagura of the age of the gods) or 'Sato Kagura' (village kagura). In Misaki itself, it is called 'Men Kagura' (mask kagura) because it is danced in masks. It is performed as an offering in the kagura hall every November.
history: The Men Kagura of Kainan Shrine was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Miura City on 21 January 1971 (Showa 46). Today it is carried on by the Kainan Shrine Men Kagura performers' association.

Men Kagura is performed as an offering after the [[出居戸祭]] festival. This festival is held on the first Day of the Sheep in November, the day on which the shrine's main deity, Lord Fujiwara no Sukemitsu, is said to have drifted ashore at Misaki. The chief priest of Kainan Shrine says that Men Kagura seems to have its roots in an old practice: Shinto priests once danced kagura in masks at the [[出居戸祭]] festival.

As befits Misaki, a town that has prospered with fishing, the kagura also has plays that pray for safety at sea and good catches. The Miura City Board of Education recorded this kagura in a two-volume book, 'The Men Kagura of Kainan Shrine' (1991 and 1992).
features: Yudate kagura (a hot-water rite) is held on the first Day of the Sheep in November. Men Kagura is then performed as an offering on the next day, the Day of the Monkey, and on the day after, the Day of the Rooster.
The plays include 'Kunigatame', 'Ebisu no Mai', 'Rashomon', 'Oeyama', 'Orochi Taiji' and 'Iwato Biraki'. About ten plays are chosen from these and performed.

programs.name: Kunigatame (making the land firm)
programs.text: This play always opens Men Kagura. It is based on Japan's myths of the creation of the world.

programs.name: Ebisu no Mai (Ebisu's dance)
programs.text: Ebisu, the guardian god of the sea, is shown landing a big sea bream. The play prays for safe fishing and good catches, and is typical of Misaki.

programs.name: Urashima Taro
programs.text: Like Ebisu no Mai, this play has been performed to pray for good catches. It is regarded as a play found only in Misaki, a town that grew up around fishing.

programs.name: Sannin-bayashi (three musicians)
programs.text: In this play, the 'Taihei no Mai' (dance of great peace) is danced to pray for peace in the world.

programs.name: Orochi Taiji (slaying the serpent)
programs.text: This play acts out the myth in which Susanoo makes the serpent Orochi drunk on sake and then slays it.

programs.name: Iwato Biraki (opening the Rock Cave)
programs.text: This play closes Men Kagura. It ends when Amaterasu appears from inside the rock cave.

viewing: The performances are at night. Misaki is a seaside town, so dress warmly.

鶴岡八幡宮の御神楽.tagline: Mikagura performed with the restored 'Miyabito' melody
鶴岡八幡宮の御神楽.intro: This is the 'mikagura' (court-style kagura) performed every year on 16 December at Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine in Kamakura, Kanagawa Prefecture, during the Gochinza Kinensai, the festival commemorating the enshrinement of the deity. The restored 'Miyabito' melody is performed as kagura handed down from around the time the shrine was founded, and the bugaku court dance 'Ninjo no Mai' is also offered.
history: The Gochinza Kinensai commemorates 1191 (Kenkyu 2), the year Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine was laid out in its present form. The date recorded in the chronicle 'Azuma Kagami', 21 November, has been converted to today's calendar, so the festival is held on 16 December.
features: This kagura follows the tradition of the mikagura handed down at the Imperial Court. It is distinguished from the 'sato kagura' (village kagura) danced at festivals of ordinary shrines. The mikagura of the Imperial Court is not open to the public, but the Ninjo dance offered at Tsurugaoka Hachimangu can be seen.

A Shinto rite is held in the main shrine at 5 p.m. After that, everyone moves to the garden on the north side of the dance pavilion, and the kagura is performed there. The dancing takes place in the light of bonfires.

Mikagura is originally a suite in three parts: a main part that welcomes the gods, a middle part in which people make merry together with the gods, and a closing part that sends the gods off. The Ninjo dance is accompanied by the kagura flute, the hichiriki (a reed pipe) and the wagon (a Japanese zither).

programs.name: Miyabito-mai (dance to the Miyabito melody)
programs.text: According to the 'Azuma Kagami', the 'Miyabito' melody was sung by O no Yoshikata, a court musician invited from Kyoto, when the deity was moved to the new shrine in 1191. The melody has been restored, and this dance is performed to it.

programs.name: Ninjo-mai (dance of the ninjo, the leader)
programs.text: This dance is performed by the 'ninjo', who leads the mikagura. The dancer wears a white robe and holds a branch of sakaki (a sacred tree) hung with a white ring. Watch for this solemn figure.

viewing: The festival starts in the evening. The shrine grounds get cold, so dress warmly.

早池峰神楽.tagline: 'Yamabushi' kagura handed down by two kagura troupes, Take and Otsugunai
早池峰神楽.intro: Hayachine Kagura is the collective name for Take Kagura and Otsugunai Kagura in Ohasama, Hanamaki, Iwate Prefecture. It is said to have been handed down by the 'yamabushi' (mountain ascetics) of Mount Hayachine. The dancing always ends with the 'Gongen-mai' (dance of the sacred lion head). It is an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan and is also inscribed as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.
history: No written records survive. However, Hayachine Shrine in Take holds a lion head inscribed with the year 1595 (Bunroku 4), and Otsugunai holds a document dated 1488 (Chokyo 2) on the handing down of the kagura. From these, the kagura is thought to go back to the Nanbokucho period (the period of the Northern and Southern Courts), and it is said to have a history of more than 500 years. Faith in Mount Hayachine is old, and it is also said that the kagura grew out of prayer dances performed by yamabushi of the Shugendo tradition.

Take Kagura is the kagura offered at Hayachine Shrine. Some say it was passed on from the 'hoin' (yamabushi priests) of Shimohei District or Miyako, but its origins are unclear. Otsugunai Kagura is the kagura offered at Otsugunai Shrine. It is said to have been passed to the 'betto' family (the shrine stewards) of Otsugunai from the priest of Tanaka Myojin, a shrine built by Tanaka Hyobu, who is regarded as the founder who opened Mount Hayachine as a sacred mountain. Many 'deshi kagura' (disciple kagura), which learned their art from the two troupes, are also found, mainly around Hanamaki.
features: There are more than 40 plays. Take and Otsugunai sometimes use different names for them, but the content is almost the same.

A performance begins with the 'Uchinarashi', which calls down the gods. After six 'shikimai' (ritual dances), a few pieces are chosen from the dances of the gods, women's dances, fierce dances, bangaku dances and others. Comic 'kyogen' pieces are sometimes included.
A short play lasts about 15 minutes, and a long one can run for more than 40 minutes.

Take Kagura is described as fast and bold, with a five-beat rhythm. Otsugunai Kagura is described as slow and graceful, with a seven-beat rhythm. The curtains hung on the stage also differ: Take uses a pattern of facing cranes, and Otsugunai uses chrysanthemum and paulownia patterns.

programs.name: Tori-mai (bird dance)
programs.text: This is the first of the shikimai. Two unmasked dancers dance holding fans and other objects. The chicken is regarded as a bird that drives away evil spirits, and the dance is thought to purify the stage. In Take Kagura the dancer wearing the hen headdress appears first; in Otsugunai Kagura it is the dancer wearing the rooster headdress.

programs.name: Sanbaso
programs.text: This is the third of the shikimai. An old man in a black mask enters lightly and announces himself in a comic way. Compared with the slow Okina dance (dance of the old man), it has a fast tempo and some acrobatic movements, which make it popular.

programs.name: Hachiman-mai (Hachiman dance)
programs.text: Two unmasked dancers enter with bows in their left hands and arrows at their waists. The dance praises the origins of the great god Hachiman and the virtues of the bow and arrow. It is regarded as a prayer dance in which arrows are shot in all four directions to drive away evil.

programs.name: Yama-no-Kami-mai (dance of the mountain god)
programs.text: The mountain god, identified with Oyamatsumi, drives away misfortune and calms it, for example by making the 'kuji' (a protective spell of nine signs). The mountain god's mask has an open mouth ('a') in Otsugunai Kagura and a closed mouth ('un') in Take Kagura, and the two kagura are said to form a pair.

programs.name: Iwato-biraki (opening the Rock Cave)
programs.text: Performed at the end of the shikimai, this play is based on the myth of the Heavenly Rock Cave. Amaterasu has shut herself in the cave, and the play shows how she is brought out by the prayer of Ame-no-Koyane, the dance of Ame-no-Uzume and the strength of Ame-no-Tajikarao.

programs.name: Gongen-mai (dance of the sacred lion head)
programs.text: This dance is always performed at the very end of the kagura. It drives away all kinds of misfortune and prays for people's safety, and it is held in especially high regard. The lion head is treated as 'Gongen-sama', an incarnation of the god. Prayer rites such as 'mi-gatame' (protecting the body) and 'hibuse' (protection from fire) are sometimes performed.

viewing: The second Sunday of every month is 'Kagura Day'. At the Ohasama Exchange and Revitalisation Centre (Hayachine Hall), Take Kagura, Otsugunai Kagura and Yagimaki Kagura take turns to perform, a different troupe each month (admission 1,000 yen, starts at 11 a.m.).

The first performances of the new year ('maizome') are held by Otsugunai Kagura on 2 January at the Kagura no Yakata (kagura house), and by Take Kagura on 3 January at Hayachine Shrine. Check the dates with the Hanamaki Tourism Association or another source before you go.

There are several shrines with similar names around Mount Hayachine. Hayachine Shrine in Tono, whose name is written with a slightly different character, is a different shrine. If you are driving, check your destination setting carefully.

南部神楽.tagline: Theatrical kagura in which the dancers speak lines
南部神楽.intro: This kagura is found from southern Iwate Prefecture to northern Miyagi Prefecture (the northern part of the Sendai domain in the Edo period). It comes from the tradition of 'yamabushi' kagura (kagura of the mountain ascetics), but its special feature is its drama dances, in which the dancers proclaim their lines in loud voices. For this reason it is also called 'Serifu Kagura' (kagura with spoken lines). It was carried on by local people who loved kagura.
history: It is said to have been created when local farmers and others added comic, kyogen-like drama dances to the older 'hoin' kagura and yamabushi kagura. They took these from 'oku-joruri' (a form of chanted storytelling), legends and other sources. In the Edo period, people other than religious figures were forbidden to perform kagura. Partly for this reason, it is thought to have grown out of kagura lovers enjoying it among friends. At the end of the Edo period the restrictions were relaxed. When Shugendo was abolished at the start of the Meiji era, the yamabushi (hoin) lost their power, and farmers freely formed kagura groups and created their own kagura.

Although its name contains 'Nanbu', it is found in the former Sendai (Date) domain. The folk performing arts researcher Honda Yasuji wrote that it is called Nanbu Kagura in the Sendai domain and Sendai Kagura in the Nanbu domain. In Iwate Prefecture it is most common in Ichinoseki and the Isawa area of Oshu, and in Miyagi Prefecture in Kurihara. At the foot of Mount Jikyo in Hagisho, Ichinoseki, a stone monument marks 'the source of Nanbu Kagura'.
features: The 'shikimai' (ritual dances) offered to the gods and the stage set-up keep the religious character of yamabushi and hoin kagura. In the other pieces, the drama dances, the dancers speak lines, and these are rich in entertainment.
The drama dances tell stories such as those of the Genpei War (between the Minamoto and Taira clans). A key feature is that they are strongly enjoyed as drama, like plays in a theatre.

The gongen-mai (lion-head dance) of yamabushi kagura and the yudate (hot-water rite) of hoin kagura have not been taken in. On the other hand, costumes with bold designs and colours, and a folk-song style of singing and speaking, are said to be elements newly born in Nanbu Kagura.

Fusa Kagura in Ichinoseki (an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Iwate Prefecture) has made itself more entertaining by adding drama dances adapted for kagura from stories such as the 'Genpei Seisuiki' and the night attack of the Soga brothers.
One of the plays, 'Tori-mai', has been passed down by teaching it to children at primary schools in Hanaizumi, Ichinoseki.

programs.name: Tori-mai (rooster dance)
programs.text: This is the first of the shikimai. Some troupes also call it 'Mikagura'. Each area has its own features, and the way it is danced varies.

programs.name: Sanbaso
programs.text: One of the dances of the gods that come from the yamabushi kagura tradition. In Arikabe Kagura in Kannari, Kurihara, the ritual dances have been performed in the order Sanbaso, Iwato-iri (entering the Rock Cave) and Iwato-biraki (opening the Rock Cave).

programs.name: Omuro-yaki (burning the chamber)
programs.text: This is said to be one of the dances of the gods newly added in Nanbu Kagura. Sugae Masumi wrote that in 1786 (Tenmei 6), in the Edo period, a 'muro-yaki' rite acting out the story of the birth of Hikohohodemi was held at the festival of Haishiwa Shrine in Ichinoseki.

programs.name: Gikeiki (the story of Yoshitsune)
programs.text: A drama dance that tells stories about Minamoto no Yoshitsune. In the Nanbu Kagura handed down around Hiraizumi, Yoshitsune is regarded as an essential subject.

viewing: The shikimai and the drama dances have different highlights. In the drama dances, listen also to the dancers' lines and follow the story.
Check performance dates, times and plays with the organiser before you go.

岩手の神楽.tagline: Many kinds of kagura by area, from yamabushi kagura to Nanbu Kagura
岩手の神楽.intro: These are the kagura rooted in many parts of Iwate Prefecture. Each area hands down kagura with its own features: 'yamabushi' kagura brought by the yamabushi (mountain ascetics), 'miyaburi' kagura performed by Shinto priests, and Nanbu Kagura, in which the dancers speak lines. Among the prefecture's folk performing arts, kagura is the third most common, after 'shishi-odori' (deer dances) and 'kenbai' (sword dances).
history: Iwate has sacred mountains such as Mount Hayachine, Mount Iwate and Mount Himekami, and many yamabushi were active there. The prefecture's yamabushi kagura is said to have been brought around the medieval period by yamabushi who travelled from place to place for their training. In the Edo period, Nanbu Toshitaka, the 10th lord of the Morioka domain and a devout believer in Shinto, named the kagura performed by families of Shinto priests 'miyaburi kagura'. He also sent Shinto priests to Edo to learn the kagura of Edo.

When Shinto and Buddhism were separated at the start of the Meiji era and Shugendo declined, some yamabushi-type kagura was changed into Shinto-priest-type kagura. In the former Date domain in the south of the prefecture, farmers created Nanbu Kagura based on the kagura of the 'hoin' (yamabushi priests). Farming and fishing are important here, and the wish to thank the gods and pray for good harvests and good catches is said to have supported kagura to this day.
features: Yamabushi kagura is the most common type in the prefecture. A lion head is enshrined as 'Gongen', and the 'gongen-mai' (lion-head dance) drives away misfortune and prays for protection from fire, rich harvests of the five grains, and good health.

Hayachine Kagura in Hanamaki, Kuromori Kagura in Miyako and Unotori Kagura in Fudai are all classed as yamabushi kagura. Many 'disciple kagura', which inherited their art from Hayachine Kagura, are also found, mainly around Hanamaki.
Kuromori Kagura and Unotori Kagura still go on kagura tours, carrying the lion head to houses along the Sanriku coast and performing the gongen-mai.

In the former Waga area of Kitakami and Hanamaki, 'Daijo Kagura' is handed down. It takes in the magic rites of Shugendo and has a strong focus on prayer. Waga Daijo Kagura in Kitakami is an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Iwate Prefecture.
In Ichinoseki and other parts of the south of the prefecture, Nanbu Kagura is handed down. Besides the 'shikimai' (ritual dances), it has drama dances in which the dancers speak lines.

programs.name: Gongen-mai (dance of the sacred lion head)
programs.text: The most important dance in yamabushi kagura. In Hayachine Kagura it is always performed at the end of the kagura and is treated as a dance of especially high standing.

programs.name: Tori-mai (bird dance / rooster dance)
programs.text: A play that comes from the yamabushi kagura tradition. It has also been taken into the Nanbu Kagura of the south of the prefecture, along with Sanbaso and other plays.

programs.name: Iwato-biraki (opening the Rock Cave)
programs.text: A play about the appearance of Amaterasu. In Kuromori Kagura in Miyako, one of the central plays danced at night kagura is a dance of this Rock Cave type.

programs.name: Yama-no-Kami-mai (dance of the mountain god)
programs.text: In Kuromori Kagura in Miyako, it is danced after a comic kyogen piece with a clown. It is danced together with the Ebisu-mai as a play linked to the work of the local people.

programs.name: Ebisu-mai (Ebisu's dance)
programs.text: A dance of the gods that tells how Hiruko is ordered by Amaterasu to become the guardian god of fishing, as Ebisu. It is one of the plays of Hayachine Kagura. Ebisu is also known as a god of business success.

viewing: Iwate Prefecture publishes 'Kagura Performance Information', which lists the dates and venues of kagura performances across the prefecture. It is a useful guide when choosing where to go.
At events where several troupes appear, such as local performing arts festivals, you can compare kagura of different types.
Venues and times can change. Check with the organiser before you go.

青森の神楽.tagline: Yamabushi kagura with the gongen-mai, the nomai of Shimokita, and Tsugaru Kagura danced by Shinto priests
青森の神楽.intro: Aomori Prefecture has kagura with different origins depending on the area. A key feature is that the traditions are divided. In the Nanbu area in the south of the prefecture, there is 'yamabushi' kagura (kagura of the mountain ascetics) in which a lion head is worshipped as 'Gongen-sama'. On the Shimokita Peninsula, there is 'nomai' (literally 'noh dance'), brought by yamabushi of the Shugendo tradition. In the Tsugaru area, there is 'Tsugaru Kagura', danced only by Shinto priests.
history: The Nanbu area has kagura said to have been brought by yamabushi of the Shugendo tradition. Nanbu Kirita Kagura in Towada is said to have been handed down by yamabushi who served Kirita Hachimangu Shrine, a shrine linked to the Nanbu family. It was once called the core of yamabushi kagura in the Nanbu area of the prefecture. It declined for a time, but is said to have been revived in the late Edo period by learning kagura from a 'maidayu' (dance master) of Kozuya in Iwate. Okamisawa Kagura in Misawa is also thought to be yamabushi-type kagura brought by Shugendo practitioners, judging from contents such as its gongen-mai.

Tsugaru Kagura is said to have begun with Sekihachi Bungo Yasutaka of Fujisaki. He learned kagura in Edo in 1712 (Shotoku 2). After returning to his domain, he trained Shinto priests, and in 1714 (Shotoku 4) the kagura was offered at the festival of Takaoka Reisha shrine. It is performed only by Shinto priests and is regarded as a performing art of high standing.
features: In the kagura of the Nanbu area, the 'gongen-mai' (lion-head dance) is central. In the gongen-mai of Nanbu Kirita Kagura, five lion heads appear together and dance boldly to the intense rhythm of the conch shell, drum, flute and small hand cymbals.

For the nomai of Shimokita, the performers carry Gongen-sama (the lion head) from house to house at New Year, and at night they perform in community halls. It begins with the 'shikimai' (ritual dances) Tori-mai, Okina and Sanbaso, goes on to warrior dances and others, and ends with the gongen-mai, a prayer dance. It is an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
Some kagura, such as Same Kagura in Hachinohe, left the hands of the yamabushi and have been performed by boat carpenters and fishermen as entertainment for ordinary people.
Tsugaru Kagura is danced in the kagura halls and worship halls of shrines in the Tsugaru area during their festivals. Eleven plays survive today, including 'Kamiiri-mai', 'Hoken' and 'Isonami'.

programs.name: Gongen-mai (dance of the sacred lion head)
programs.text: In this dance, the lion head is danced as Gongen-sama. It is the central dance of yamabushi-type kagura in the Nanbu area. In Nanbu Kirita Kagura it is a dance of 'securing the five directions', the four directions and the centre, and it prays for driving away evil and for peace in the land.

programs.name: Tori-mai, Okina and Sanbaso (bird dance, old man and Sanbaso)
programs.text: The shikimai danced first in the nomai of Shimokita. Plays with the same names, such as Tori-mai, are also handed down in Nanbu Kirita Kagura and Takko Kagura.

programs.name: Bushi-mai (warrior dances: Yashima, the Soga Brothers and others)
programs.text: Plays with warriors as the main characters. In the nomai of Shimokita, pieces such as 'Shinobu', 'Yashima' and 'Soga Kyodai' (the Soga brothers) are performed after the shikimai. Wearing masks and costumes and holding swords and fans, the dancers perform each piece, about 30 minutes long, at a fast tempo and with great vigour.

programs.name: Kanemaki (coiled around the bell)
programs.text: A play in the nomai of Shimokita, performed alongside the warrior dances, in which humans and demonic beings are involved with each other.

programs.name: Kumimai (combined plays: Dannoura Shikorobiki, Ataka no Seki Kanjincho, Rashomon and others)
programs.text: Plays handed down in Same Kagura in Hachinohe. From around the end of the Edo period, kabuki and puppet plays were combined and adapted into kagura. Together with older pieces such as the shikimai, 34 plays are handed down.

viewing: The Aomori Prefectural Board of Education's 'Aomori Pride - Folk Performing Arts Passed on to the Future' performances are free to watch, and many of the prefecture's folk performing arts groups appear together.

When kagura is shown to the public differs from troupe to troupe, for example at a shrine's annual festival or at regular performances. Check with the local board of education or preservation society before you go.

出雲神楽.tagline: The kagura of the Izumo region, danced in three parts: Shichiza, Shikisanba and Shinno
出雲神楽.intro: This kagura was born in the Izumo region, the setting of many myths, and has been danced mainly in eastern Shimane Prefecture. It is made up of three kinds of dance: the unmasked 'Shichiza' (seven ritual dances), the celebratory 'Shikisanba', and the masked mythological dramas called 'Shinno' (god noh). In Unnan there are performances all year round.
history: This form of Izumo kagura is thought to have been shaped between the Sengoku (Warring States) period and the early Edo period, mainly by the Shinto priests of Sada Shrine (Kashima, Matsue), who also took in elements of noh and kyogen. It then spread throughout the Izumo region. 'Sada Shinno', handed down at Sada Shrine and nearby shrines, is said to have taken its present form in the Keicho era (late 16th to early 17th century): the priests learned the movements of noh in Kyoto and modelled the kagura on them. It is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.

Unnan now has 16 kagura troupes. Tsukinoya Kagura in the Tsukiya area of Kisuki is said to have learned and handed down the kagura of Izumo District in the mid-Edo period. It was designated an Intangible Cultural Property of Shimane Prefecture in 1962 (Showa 37). In addition, six Izumo kagura troupes designated as Intangible Folk Cultural Properties by Shimane Prefecture or Unnan City are component cultural properties of the Japan Heritage 'Izumo-no-kuni Tatara Fudoki - The Story Born from a Thousand Years of Ironmaking'.
features: Some Shinno plays are based on myths recorded in the 'Kojiki' and the 'Nihon Shoki', and many include stories linked to the basin of the Hii River, which flows through Unnan.

In Unnan, the myths have been handed down alongside the history of 'tatara' ironmaking (traditional furnace ironmaking). For example, Yamata-no-Orochi is likened to rivers that flooded because of iron sand mining, and the sword that came out of the slain Orochi is likened to a symbol of ironmaking.
The music (hayashi) of Sada Shinno uses the shime-daiko (a tightly laced drum), large and small hand drums, the flute and the 'tebyoshi' (literally 'hand beat'). The long-bodied drum is not used.
Tsukinoya Kagura also preserves plays not seen elsewhere, such as 'I no Hi Matsuri' (festival of the Day of the Boar) and 'Sanbo Kojin'.

programs.name: Shichiza (seven ritual dances)
programs.text: Ritual dances performed without masks, holding torimono (hand-held ritual objects). In Sada Shinno they consist of seven dances: 'Kenmai', 'Sanku', 'Goza', 'Kiyome', 'Kanjo', 'Tagusa' and 'Yaotome'.

programs.name: Shikisanba (celebratory ritual dances)
programs.text: Ceremonial dances for celebration. In Sada Shinno, 'Okina' and 'Sanbaso', taken from noh and kyogen, are danced.

programs.name: Shinno (god noh)
programs.text: Dramatic dances performed in masks, based on myths and legends. In Sada Shinno they have a dignified style modelled on noh, with a chorus. Eleven pieces are handed down, including 'Taisha' and 'Yaegaki'.

viewing: At the Kodai Tetsu Kayokan in Daito, Unnan, the city's kagura troupes take turns to appear in a regular performance, 'Izumo Kagura no Yube' (An Evening of Izumo Kagura). In fiscal year 2026 (Reiwa 8) it runs from 7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Admission is 1,000 yen for high school students and older, and free for junior high school students and younger.
The Unnan City Tourism Association gives a monthly schedule of performances by the city's kagura troupes. Check the latest information before you go.

飯南神楽.tagline: The kagura of the Iinan Kagura Troupe, which carries on Hiroshima kagura, rare in the Unnan area
飯南神楽.intro: This kagura is danced by the Iinan Kagura Troupe, based in the Tani district of Iinan, Shimane Prefecture. Unusually for the Unnan area, the troupe carries on Hiroshima kagura. It describes its own style as 'Asuna-kei hacchoshi' (the Asuna line of 'hacchoshi', a fast eight-beat rhythm). The troupe says its kagura tells stories, and its staging and costumes are showy and easy to follow, so even first-time viewers can enjoy it.
history: Iinan also has 'Okuiishi Shinshoku Kagura' (the Shinto priests' kagura of Okuiishi), a kagura of the Izumo line. It was designated by Shimane Prefecture in 1961 (Showa 36), and it is performed as an offering at Akana Hachimangu Shrine and other places.

The Iinan Kagura Troupe was formed by kagura lovers from inside and outside the town, centred on former members of the 'Tani Kodomo Kagura' (Tani children's kagura). That children's group was formed in the Showa 50s to carry on traditional performing arts. The troupe received costumes and props from the [[森島]] Kagura Troupe, a troupe in the town that had stopped its activities, and it was founded in 2005 (Heisei 17) as the 'Iinan Kagura Club'. In December 2016 (Heisei 28), on its 10th anniversary, it changed its name to the Iinan Kagura Troupe. In 2018 (Heisei 30) it presented [[程原入道]], a newly created play that turns a legend of its home district of Tani into kagura. At its 15th anniversary performance in December 2021 (Reiwa 3), it showed the new plays 'Amano Iwato' (the Heavenly Rock Cave) and 'Hachiman'. In 2026 (Reiwa 8) the troupe marks 20 years since its founding.
features: The troupe has 18 plays, including ritual dances and newly created plays. It gives about 30 performances a year, as offering kagura at annual grand festivals and similar occasions, and at events inside and outside the prefecture.
The newly created play [[程原入道]] is based on a legend, handed down in Iinan, about fugitives of the defeated Heike clan. Troupe members wrote its script from scratch.
'Jinrin' is a play handed down since the pre-war years and is called a 'kyumai' (old-style dance). Comparing it with the 'shinmai' (new-style dances) is one way to enjoy the performance.

programs.name: Kamioroshi (inviting the gods down)
programs.text: A ritual dance that invites the gods to the stage. It is said to show the basic dance forms, and it lets you feel the sacred atmosphere at the start of the kagura.

programs.name: Jinrin (the winged demon)
programs.text: Jinrin is a demon with wings who attacks from the sky at the head of a great army. Emperor Chuai defeats him with the power of the heavenly demon-quelling arrow and the bow of divine protection.

programs.name: Oeyama (Mount Oe)
programs.text: Minamoto no Yorimitsu sets out with his four great retainers ('shitenno'), disguised as 'yamabushi' (mountain ascetics), and slays Shuten Doji of Mount Oe. A highlight is the exchange of questions and answers between Yorimitsu, in his yamabushi disguise, and Doji.

programs.name: A new play about a lay monk ('nyudo')
programs.text: A newly created play. [[遊那御前]], the wife of Taira no Noritsune, and their son [[教本]] flee to [[程原]] (today [[井戸谷]] in Iinan). [[教本]] slays a great serpent ('orochi'), later becomes a monk and takes the name [[程原入道]]. The play follows this story.
