viewing: If you want to post photos of the Iinan Kagura Troupe's performances on social media or elsewhere, you must ask troupe members directly for permission for each performance. Posting videos is, as a rule, not allowed.
Upcoming performances are announced one by one on the Iinan Kagura Troupe's official website. Some performances are not open to the general public, so check before you go.

豊前神楽.area: The Keichiku area of Fukuoka Prefecture and other areas
豊前神楽.tagline: Kagura of the former Buzen Province, where the demon 'Misaki' plays a leading part
豊前神楽.intro: This kagura has been performed as an offering at shrines of the former Buzen Province, centred on the Keichiku area in north-eastern Fukuoka Prefecture. One of its features is that many plays include the demon role called 'Misaki'. In 2016 (Heisei 28) it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan under the name 'Buzen Kagura'. Thirty kagura groups are still active in the Keichiku area today.
history: Its origins are unclear, but it appears in records by the early Edo period. Until the Edo period it was handed down by Shinto priests. From the Meiji era on, private kagura associations ('kagura-ko' or 'kagura kosha') have carried it on and performed it as an offering at shrines in many places. The Keichiku area has many mountains of 'shugen' (mountain asceticism), Mount Kubote among them, and their influence can be seen in plays such as the yudate kagura (hot-water rite). Influence from 'Matsue', a festival of Buzen shugendo, is also recognised. Mountain ascetics are thought to have been deeply involved in how this kagura took shape.

It was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan on 2 March 2016 (Heisei 28). The body that protects it is the Buzen Kagura Preservation Federation of Fukuoka and Oita Prefectures. In the Keichiku area, 28 of the 30 groups are active as designated groups.
features: The plays are divided into two kinds. 'Shiki kagura' (ceremonial kagura, or kagura that brings down the gods) purifies the place and invites the gods. 'Hono kagura' (offering kagura, also called 'age kagura') is danced at the request of local parishioners.
An old form of offering survives: on the day, people making a prayer pay an offering fee for each play they want, and those plays are then danced in turn.
In the yudate kagura, a demon climbs a sacred pole about 10 metres tall set up in the shrine grounds. There is also fire-walking: walking barefoot over charcoal.
The music mainly uses three kinds of instruments: drums, small gongs and flutes.
At the shrines that the kagura associations visit, the worship halls are built with use as a kagura stage in mind. For example, they have dressing rooms attached.

programs.name: Ichiban Kagura (the first kagura)
programs.text: A solemn torimono kagura danced by four dancers without masks, holding paper wands and fans. It is a dance that worships the gods of the five elements.

programs.name: Misaki Kagura
programs.text: This play turns into kagura a scene from the myth of the heavenly grandson's descent to earth: Ame-no-Uzume meets Sarutahiko, who wears a demon mask. Plays in which Misaki appears are regarded as symbolic of Buzen Kagura.

programs.name: Ran Misaki Kagura (the wild Misaki)
programs.text: A Misaki kagura danced by two demons and two dancers who carry paper wands. In the 'yaboyabo' part, the wand dancers and the demons make friends again, put their arms around each other's shoulders and jump about. The demons chase worshippers' children and hand out mandarin oranges and sweets.

programs.name: Bon Kagura (the tray kagura)
programs.text: Holding a tray of rice in one hand, the dancer entertains worshippers with a dance like an acrobatic act. It is danced to pray for a good rice harvest.

programs.name: Yudate Kagura (hot-water rite)
programs.text: A large-scale kagura with a strong element of prayer, performed in a sacred ritual area set up in the shrine grounds.

programs.name: Iwato-biraki (opening the Heavenly Rock Cave)
programs.text: A play based on the myth of the Heavenly Rock Cave. It is regarded as the most important play in Buzen Kagura and is danced at the end of the offering.

viewing: Offering kagura is performed by the local parishioners to thank the gods and to pray for the safety of their households. Please watch in a way that does not trouble the local people.
When taking photos, avoid flash, excessive shutter noise and blocking other people's view. Take particular care if you use a tripod.

Offering kagura goes on until late at night. It gets cold, so wear clothes that are easy to adjust. A folding chair or something similar is handy. For details of dates, contact the city or town where the kagura group is based.

豊後神楽.area: Bungo-Ono, Oita Prefecture, and other areas
豊後神楽.tagline: 'Ono-kei Iwato Kagura', with Ontake Kagura as its original form
豊後神楽.intro: This kagura has been handed down mainly in Bungo-Ono, Oita Prefecture, and is also called 'Ono-kei Iwato Kagura' (Iwato kagura of the Ono line). Its plays are based on myths from the Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), centred on the opening of the Heavenly Rock Cave. Ontake Kagura in Kiyokawa, regarded as its original form, is an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
history: Some say there was kagura in Bungo-Ono as early as the Kamakura period. However, it can only be confirmed as actually performed from the Edo period, and it is thought to have arisen under the influence of Izumo kagura. Ontake Kagura is said to have begun in 1449 (Hotoku 1), when Otomo Chikataka, the 'shugo' (military governor) of Bungo Province, invited the deity of Ontake Shrine to the area ('kanjo'). In 1778 (An'ei 7), 'kagura odori' was abolished by order of the Oka domain. [[加藤長古]], the chief priest of Ontake Shrine, then created a new kagura with a greatly changed structure. From the end of the Edo period this kagura spread to other shrines, and schools such as the Ontake, Asakusa and [[深山流]] schools arose.

When kagura by Shinto priests was banned after the Meiji Restoration, the local parishioners in the villages took it over, and kagura troupes ('kagura-za') were formed in many places. As village kagura ('sato kagura') it spread from southern to central Oita Prefecture and even to the Aso area of Kumamoto Prefecture. Ontake Kagura was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan in 2007 (Heisei 19).
features: At festivals, about 8 to 10 plays are performed as an offering before the gods. There is also 'hana kagura', which parishioners offer individually to pray for things such as their children's growth and their family's good health.
Ontake Kagura still preserves 33 plays, mainly on themes from myths.
Seventeen kagura groups are currently active in Bungo-Ono.
Yufu, home of Yufuin Onsen (hot spring), also has a dozen or so kagura troupes. Some of their kagura has been handed down for more than 200 years.

programs.name: Goho Reishi (rite of the five directions)
programs.text: At the autumn festival of Ontake Shrine, this play is always danced first. Five dancers perform a dance that is meant to purify the place.

programs.name: Shibahiki (pulling the brushwood)
programs.text: A play said to stand for preparing the sakaki (sacred evergreen) to be set up in front of the Heavenly Rock Cave.

programs.name: Tsunakiri (cutting the rope)
programs.text: A play about Susanoo slaying Yamata-no-Orochi, the eight-headed serpent.

programs.name: Iwato-biraki (opening the Heavenly Rock Cave)
programs.text: A play based on the myth of Amaterasu, who hid herself in the rock cave.

programs.name: Ukei (the sacred vow)
programs.text: A play based on the myth of 'ukei', in which Amaterasu and Susanoo make solemn vows.

programs.name: Taijin (the great god)
programs.text: This play is always danced at the end of the festival. It is said to give thanks that the kagura has ended safely and to celebrate peace throughout the land.

viewing: At the Kagura Kaikan (kagura hall) in Kiyokawa, Bungo-Ono, regular performances are held about once a month. Tickets can be booked at the Kagura Kaikan. Tickets bought on the day may cost more than advance tickets (500 yen more for the December 2026 performance).

In Yufuin Onsen, 'Yufuin Onsen Kagura: the monthly offering' is held once a month. The venue, Otomaru Community Centre, is a 3-minute walk from JR Yufuin Station. Admission is free and no booking is needed. If you come by car, use a paid car park nearby.
Every autumn, the Ontake-ryu Kagura Festival (a festival of the Ontake school of kagura) is held at the park [[能場公園]] in Kiyokawa, the birthplace of Ontake Kagura. In 2026 it is the 39th festival.

江戸里神楽.tagline: Village kagura with roots in Edo, acting out myths as masked plays without words
江戸里神楽.intro: This 'sato kagura' (village kagura) has been performed since the Edo period by professional kagura performers at shrine festivals in Edo (the old name of Tokyo) and the surrounding area. Its main feature is wordless mime: the performers wear masks and act out stories from myths without speaking. Today four troupes carry it on, the Wakayama, Mamiya, Matsumoto and Yamamoto troupes, and it is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
history: It is said to have started with the 'Haji Ichiryu Saibara Kagura' of Washinomiya Shrine (Saitama Prefecture), which was brought to Edo in the early Edo period. It flourished most in the Bunka and Bunsei eras (1804-30). After the Meiji Restoration many of its performers scattered, but it is said that 37 families still remained in Edo in the early Meiji era.

Their number fell further after that. Today four troupes remain active: the Wakayama troupe (Taito Ward), the Mamiya troupe (Shinagawa Ward), the Matsumoto troupe (Arakawa Ward) and the Yamamoto troupe (Inagi). It was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan on 13 December 1994 (Heisei 6). The Yamamoto Yorinobu troupe of Inagi says that its first head began it in 1373 (Oan 6), in the early Muromachi period.
features: Its core is mime-like plays based on myths and performed in masks, such as 'Ame-no-Ukihashi' (the Floating Bridge of Heaven) and 'Ame-no-Kaeshiya' (the returned arrow). They are said to have been developed from the kagura of Washinomiya Shrine under the influence of Mibu Kyogen from Kyoto.
Later, plays based on kabuki, noh and folk tales were also added, such as 'Tsuri Onna' (fishing for a wife), 'Momijigari' (maple viewing) and 'Urashima Taro'.

The troupes do not belong to any particular shrine. They have performed on request from local parishioners and others, in the kagura halls (dance halls) of shrines in many places, at annual grand festivals and other occasions.
Another feature of Edo sato kagura is that its performers are full-time professional kagura performers.

programs.name: Yakumo Shin'ei (slaying the serpent)
programs.text: Susanoo has been banished to Ne-no-Kuni (the Land of Roots). He is moved when he hears the grief of Kushinada-hime and her parents, and he slays Yamata-no-Orochi, the eight-headed serpent.

programs.name: Tenson Korin (the descent of the heavenly grandson)
programs.text: As Ninigi is about to descend to the earth, a frightening god with a long nose appears before him. When Ame-no-Uzume asks his name, he turns out to be Sarutahiko, who has come to guide them. Led by Sarutahiko, the party descends to the land of Hyuga.

programs.name: Hohi no Shinshi (Hohi the envoy)
programs.text: Ame-no-Hohi goes down to Okuninushi as an envoy, to ask him to hand over the land. But he falls for a trick, gives himself up to drinking sake and fails to report back to Takamagahara (the Plain of High Heaven).

programs.name: Ame-no-Kaeshiya (the returned arrow)
programs.text: The next envoy, Ame-no-Wakahiko, also forgets his task after marrying Okuninushi's daughter. He shoots an arrow at the pheasant that has come for him. The play follows the story until that arrow is thrown back from Takamagahara and strikes Wakahiko himself.

programs.name: Kumaso Seibatsu (conquering the Kumaso)
programs.text: Prince Ousu dresses as a woman in clothes given to him by his aunt Yamatohime. In this disguise he gets close to Kumaso Takeru and kills him. For this deed he takes the new name Yamato Takeru.

programs.name: Shinden Tanemaki (sowing the sacred field)
programs.text: A fox sows the seeds of the five grains and pounds rice cakes, while a 'modoki' (a comic imitator) digs them up and sneaks bites to eat. At the end an old man who is a Shinto priest appears and takes back the sacred tools from the modoki.

viewing: At Okunitama Shrine in Fuchu, Edo sato kagura is performed as an offering three times, at 3 pm, 5 pm and 7 pm, on the days of the Tori-no-Ichi fair (according to the 2026 notice).
At Anazawa Tenjin Shrine in Inagi, you can see it in the kagura hall from around 1 pm at the annual grand festival, held on the Sunday closest to and before 25 August.
Times may change from year to year, so check each shrine's notices before you go.

都々古別神社の御神楽.tagline: The 'Shichiza no Kagura' (seven-piece kagura) and 'Daidai Kagura', danced in the worship hall at the Shimotsuki Grand Festival
都々古別神社の御神楽.intro: This sacred kagura is performed as an offering in the worship hall of Yatsuki Tsutsukowake Shrine in Tanagura, Fukushima Prefecture. It is held every year at the Shimotsuki Grand Festival ('shimotsuki' means the eleventh month) on the second Saturday and Sunday of December. To pray for a rich harvest of the five grains and other blessings, the 'Shichiza no Kagura' (seven-piece kagura) and the 'Daidai Kagura' are danced. It is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Fukushima Prefecture.
history: Around the Edo period, Yatsuki Tsutsukowake Shrine, Baba Tsutsukowake Shrine and Shimomiya Chikatsu Shrine were together called the 'Chikatsu Sansha' (the three Chikatsu shrines). Yatsuki Tsutsukowake Shrine is the middle shrine of the three. Its former name was Chikatsu Daimyojin, and it was given its present name in Meiji 18 (the 18th year of the Meiji era). Many kinds of rituals and performing arts have been handed down at the shrine since long ago.

At the Shimotsuki Grand Festival, there is said to have been a custom of offering that year's new unhulled rice wrapped in straw bundles ('tsutokko'), and taking home someone else's tsutokko. This custom reflects the shrine's character as a shrine to a god of farming. The kagura was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Fukushima Prefecture on 23 March 1979 (Showa 54), under the name 'Kagura of Yatsuki Tsutsukowake Shrine'.
features: According to Fukushima Prefecture, kagura of the Izumo line, with beautiful music, has been handed down at this shrine, and the 'Shichiza no Kagura' is part of it.
Besides the Daidai Kagura, the plays include [[幣舞]], [[白枚舞]], [[弓舞]], [[剣舞]], [[神扇舞]], [[粆舞]] and [[神子]] (a lion dance). Two or three of them are performed at the Shimotsuki Grand Festival.
The Yatsuki Tsutsukowake Shrine Gakujin Association, the group of shrine musicians who carry on the tradition, also helps with efforts to pass it on at local primary schools.
On the festival days, the 'Yatsuki Ichi' market of stalls sets up in and around the shrine grounds. It is busy with visitors buying the local specialities, yuzu citrus and ginger.

programs.name: Paper wand dance
programs.text: Two 'gakujin' (shrine musicians) hold paper wands and bells. They first make stamping steps called 'yotsu', then dance. It is also called by a name meaning 'the wand dance that invites the gods'.

programs.name: Yumimai (bow dance)
programs.text: Two gakujin hold bows and stamp the yotsu steps. As they dance, they shoot arrows to the four directions.

programs.name: Kenmai (sword dance)
programs.text: Danced by three gakujin. One holds a paper wand and a bell, and the other two hold swords and bells and show their skill with the sword.

programs.name: Sacred fan dance and rice-scattering dance
programs.text: Two gakujin dance with bells in their hands. Then they take washed rice and scatter it as they dance.

viewing: Tanagura Town's information does not give the times of the kagura offerings. Before you go, check with Yatsuki Tsutsukowake Shrine (0247-33-3505) or the Tanagura Town Revitalisation, Tourism and Local Products Association (0247-33-7886).
There is parking for about 20 cars. The shrine is about a 13-minute walk (about 900 m) from Chikatsu Station on the JR Suigun Line.
This is a December event, so dress warmly. It is a local festival, so take care not to get in the way of worship or the rituals.

湯立神楽.area: Hamamatsu, Shizuoka Prefecture, and other areas
湯立神楽.tagline: Kagura that offers hot water from a cauldron to the gods and sprinkles it on people to purify them
湯立神楽.intro: In this kagura, water is brought to a rolling boil in a cauldron and offered to the gods. The hot water is then also sprinkled on people to purify them. In the mountains from southern Nagano Prefecture to the borders with Aichi and Shizuoka, many 'shimotsuki kagura' (kagura of the eleventh month) centred on yudate (the hot-water rite) are handed down. 'Kawai Hana-no-Mai', handed down at Yasaka Shrine in Tenryu Ward, Hamamatsu, Shizuoka Prefecture, is one of the yudate kagura of this San'en-Nanshin area.
history: The Agency for Cultural Affairs describes yudate kagura as follows. At the end of the year (shimotsuki, the eleventh month), a hearth is built and water is boiled and offered to the gods. The water is then sprinkled on people to purify their souls, and sacred songs are sung and danced as well. In some cases, the yudate and dances are repeated in turn, and then dances follow in which performers wear masks of demons and other figures.

Kawai Hana-no-Mai, handed down at Yasaka Shrine in Kawai, Sakuma-cho, Tenryu Ward, Hamamatsu, is a performing art linked to the Hana Matsuri (flower festival) of Oku-Mikawa. In Shizuoka Prefecture it is called 'Hana-no-Mai' (flower dance). The name is said to come from the impression made by the flower hats that children wear in the Mittsu-mai and Yottsu-mai dances. On 1 January 1976 (Showa 51), it was designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Shizuoka Prefecture.
features: Yudate kagura takes many forms depending on the place. In some, such as the 'Yudate Kagura of Numata and Osaka' in Gotemba, Shizuoka Prefecture, a shishi (lion) performs the yudate.

At Kawai Hana-no-Mai, a square dance area two 'ken' on each side ('ken' is a traditional unit of length) is marked off with sacred ropes (shimenawa) in front of the worship hall of Yasaka Shrine. A cauldron for the yudate is placed in the centre. Above the cauldron hangs a 'yubuta' (canopy) decorated with paper cut-outs called 'kiriko', and the performances take place around it.

After the children's flower dances, a red demon called 'Oni-sama' appears. He wears a large demon mask, holds a broad axe and stamps the 'henbai' (ritual stamping steps). In the final 'Yu-bayashi', the dancers use bundles called 'yutabusa' to sprinkle the hot water from the cauldron on the spectators.
Kawai Hana-no-Mai is performed as an offering every year on the last Saturday of October. Of the yudate kagura in the San'en-Nanshin area, it is the earliest to be held each year.

programs.name: Hana-no-Mai (flower dance: Mittsu-mai and Yottsu-mai)
programs.text: Children dance wearing flower hats. The name 'Hana-no-Mai' is also said to come from this.

programs.name: Oni-sama (the red demon)
programs.text: A red demon in a large demon mask stamps the henbai with a broad axe in his hand. It is said that if he steps wrongly, misfortune will come to the village.

programs.name: Yu-bayashi (the hot-water finale)
programs.text: To close, the dancers use yutabusa to sprinkle the boiling water from the cauldron on the spectators.

viewing: Kawai Hana-no-Mai continues from around 2 pm until late at night (according to Hamamatsu City's guide for 2026 (Reiwa 8)).

Spectators also join in the festival by calling out 'Te-hohe, tehohe'. In the Yu-bayashi, hot water from the cauldron is sprinkled on the crowd, so it is wise to wear clothes you do not mind getting wet.
Before you go, check the dates and times in the guide from the Hamamatsu City Cultural Properties Division (053-457-2466).

番楽.tagline: Shugendo kagura handed down by mountain ascetics, danced by entering and leaving through a curtain
番楽.intro: This is a kagura of the Shugendo (mountain asceticism) tradition, handed down in Akita Prefecture and the northern part of Yamagata Prefecture. It is said to have been brought by 'yamabushi' (mountain ascetics). It belongs to the same group as the yamabushi kagura of Iwate Prefecture and the 'nomai' of Aomori Prefecture. The dancers enter and leave through a curtain hung in front of the deity, and perform a wide range of plays, such as ritual dances, warrior dances and women's dances.
history: Yamabushi kagura was handed down by yamabushi (Shugendo practitioners) who were based on the sacred mountains of the Tohoku region. They revered a lion head ('shishigashira') as a 'gongen', a manifestation of the deity. In the past the name was also written with other characters, but today it is almost always written in the same way. Set plays are danced first, and then other plays are performed in turn ('ban') to suit the occasion. It is thought that this is why it came to be called bangaku.

Honkai Shishimai Bangaku is said to have been brought to the villages of Chokai-machi in the early Edo period, in the Kan'ei era (1624-1644). It was brought by Honkai Gyonin (Honkai-bo), a Shugendo practitioner who belonged to Sanbo-in of Daigo-ji Temple in Kyoto. It is still kept alive by the 'koju' (local confraternities) of 13 districts of Chokai-machi. On 9 March 2011 (Heisei 23), it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan. In various places at the northern foot of Mt Chokai, there are also bangaku that are said to have come from Honkai Shishimai Bangaku.
features: The dancers enter and leave through the middle of a curtain hung in front of the deity or in a similar place. The first day of the year on which it is performed is called 'makuaki' (curtain opening), and the last day is called 'makuosame' (curtain closing).

Besides ritual dances such as Okina and Sanbaso, the plays include warrior dances, women's dances, comic dances in the style of kyogen and more. The music (hayashi) often uses drums, gongs and flutes.

Honkai Shishimai Bangaku places special importance on the lion dance, which is always danced before the other bangaku pieces. It is danced by two people: one holds the lion head and the other holds the curtain. The movements are vigorous, and the 'ha-uchi', striking the upper and lower teeth together, is repeated many times.

According to records handed down in each koju, such as the 'Honkai-ryu Shishimai Hiden Daiji', Honkai Shishimai Bangaku has 48 plays in total. Today about 30 of them survive across all the koju combined.
It is performed at the festivals of each district's shrine, at Bon in August and at autumn harvest festivals. It is sometimes also danced to protect a newly built house from fire.

programs.name: Shishimai (lion dance)
programs.text: A vigorous dance performed by two people, with repeated ha-uchi (teeth striking). In Honkai Shishimai Bangaku it is danced before the other bangaku pieces.

viewing: Every August, Yurihonjo City holds the 'Chokai Shishi Matsuri' (Chokai lion festival), where the koju of Honkai Shishimai Bangaku perform their dances (16 August in 2026).

Performances in each district are held together with shrine festivals and similar events. Before you go, check with the Lifelong Learning Division of the Yurihonjo City Board of Education (0184-32-1332) or other contacts.
There are also chances to see it on stages outside the local area, such as the National Folk Performing Arts Festival held in Tokyo.

椎葉神楽.tagline: Danced through the winter night in each mountain hamlet
椎葉神楽.intro: This kagura is handed down in the districts of Shiiba, a mountain village in north-western Miyazaki Prefecture that borders Kumamoto Prefecture. Even today, it is performed as an offering at about 26 places in the village every year from November to December, at the grand festivals of the district shrines. Most performances go on all night. It was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan in 1991 (Heisei 3).
history: No reliable records of its origin have been found. However, the Tsugao district has a story that, around the Tensho era, the district's Shinto priest learned kagura from Aso Shrine in Higo and brought it back. The same district also still has a kagura mask with ink writing dated Kan'ei 9 (1632).

Because the area is in the mountains, far from the plains, it was little affected by the Meiji-era movement against Buddhism ('haibutsu kishaku'). The kagura still carries an old character in which Shinto gods and Buddhas are mixed together. In 1980 (Showa 55), it was selected as an intangible folk cultural property that should be recorded, and surveys were carried out. On 21 February 1991, it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
features: The ritual space is called the 'mikoya'. In the past, private homes were used, but today the worship halls of shrines and similar buildings are used. An altar called 'Takamagahara' (the High Plain of Heaven) is set up, sacred ropes ('shime') are hung all around, and a canopy-like decoration called 'kumo' is hung from the ceiling.

First, offerings such as wild boar and deer are prepared and the paper offerings ('hei') are cut. The kagura then begins with welcoming the gods ('kami-mukae'), and plays based on a basic set of thirty-three follow. It closes with sending off the gods ('kami-okuri').

The plays fall broadly into two groups. In 'torimono-mai', dancers hold torimono (hand-held ritual objects) such as paper wands, bells, folding fans, sakaki branches, swords and bows. In 'men-no-mai', dancers wear masks of demon gods and other figures. A highlight is the sight of one to four dancers dancing boldly with large movements.

The 'shogyo' are chanted words that explain the true Buddhist identity of the gods ('honji') and the meaning of the torimono. They keep an old form of the mixing of Shinto and Buddhism. The tempo of the dances and the plays differ slightly from district to district.

programs.name: Torimono-mai (dances with hand-held objects)
programs.text: Plays danced holding objects such as paper wands, bells, folding fans, sakaki branches, swords and bows.

programs.name: Men-no-mai (masked dances)
programs.text: Plays danced wearing masks of demon gods and other figures.

programs.name: Kami-okuri (sending off the gods)
programs.text: At the end of the all-night kagura, the gods are sent off and the festival is closed.

viewing: Kagura is a sacred annual festival of each hamlet. Watch it in the spirit of joining a local festival.
Local custom is for each person to bring an offering (about 2-3 'sho' of shochu; a 'sho' is a traditional unit of volume) or a cash gift (about 3,000-5,000 yen).
Get permission from the preservation society in advance before taking photos or video. Groups of 10 or more should contact the preservation society beforehand and get permission before visiting.
Performances may be cancelled or changed for local reasons. Before you go, check with the Shiiba Folk Performing Arts Museum.

巫女神楽.tagline: Shrine maidens dance with bells or flowering branches in hand and purify people
巫女神楽.intro: This is kagura danced by 'miko' (shrine maidens) at shrines. At Jonangu Shrine in Fushimi Ward, Kyoto, miko dance kagura on the front stage of the kagura hall and in the worship hall, holding seasonal flowers such as plum blossoms, wisteria and chrysanthemums. During the first three days of the New Year, they dance 'harai kagura' (purification kagura) to the sound of bells and purify the people making their first shrine visit of the year.
history: Jonangu's 'Nagoshi no Kagura' (summer purification kagura) began in Reiwa 2 (2020), when an infectious disease was spreading. A miko holds a halberd ('hoko') and performs the 'Hoko-barai no Gi' (halberd purification rite) to purify heaven and earth, and then dances the harai kagura.
features: At Jonangu, miko kagura with flowers in hand is offered in each season. In 'Umegae Kagura', the miko wears plum blossoms in her headdress and holds a plum branch. There is also 'Fuji no Miko Kagura' with wisteria flowers and 'Kiku no Miko Kagura' with chrysanthemums.

During the first three days of the New Year, from 9:00 to 16:00, miko dance the harai kagura on the front stage of the kagura hall. They purify the people making their first shrine visit of the year and pray for their good health and safety. It is performed about every 30 minutes.

At the 'Osuzumi Kagura' (kagura for enjoying the evening cool), usually held on 20 July, miko dance the harai kagura on the front stage of the kagura hall in the evening. They hold sacred bells and 'fukuzasa' (lucky bamboo branches).

programs.name: Harai Kagura (purification kagura)
programs.text: A kagura danced while ringing kagura bells, to purify people and drive away misfortune.

programs.name: Umegae Kagura (plum branch kagura)
programs.text: A miko with plum blossoms in her headdress dances holding a plum branch.

viewing: The harai kagura during the first three days of the New Year is open for anyone to watch.
During the periods of the flower miko kagura, a miko purifies each person who receives a flower amulet ('hanamamori') one by one with kagura bells (offering fee: 1,000 yen).
The dates are announced each year in Jonangu's schedule. Check them before you go.

平戸神楽.tagline: 24 plays handed down by Shinto priests, and 'Niken', danced with three real swords
平戸神楽.intro: This kagura is danced at shrine festivals in northern Nagasaki Prefecture, in the lands of the former Hirado domain, excluding Iki. Shinto priests dance to gagaku (court-style music) played on flute and drum, holding paper wands, bows, swords and other objects. There are 24 plays in all, and the number danced changes with the rank of the festival. It is designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan.
history: It is said to have begun in the Genki era (1570-1573). When Iki became a territory of the Matsura clan of Hirado, the Shinto priests of Iki visited the Matsura clan's castle in Hirado and danced the kagura of Iki's 'Kamado Matsuri' (hearth festival). It is said that the Hirado priests later joined this festival too, and that the two sides passed their skills on to each other.

The basis of its present form was laid at the beginning of the Edo period. According to tradition, in the Shoho era (1644-1648), when Matsura Shigenobu (Tensho) was lord of Hirado, Tachibana Mitsuyoshi, a Shinto priest and scholar of Japanese classics ('kokugaku'), travelled to the 'ichinomiya' (leading shrines) all over Japan and studied the kagura of each region. He then revised and added to the Hirado kagura and completed the 24 plays of Hirado Kagura.

In 1987 (Showa 62), it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan, together with Iki Kagura, which also comes from the former Hirado domain. The organisation responsible for its protection is the Hirado Kagura Promotion Association.
features: It is a 'torimono kagura', danced holding torimono (hand-held ritual objects) such as paper wands, bows and swords. It is normally danced in the worship hall or offering hall of a shrine, but a temporary stage is sometimes set up.
Depending on the rank of the festival, it is danced in one of four sizes: Kokagura (8 plays), Chukagura (12 plays), Daikagura (18 plays) and Daidaikagura (24 plays).
The music is gagaku played on flute and drum. Both the dances and the music have been handed down by Shinto priests from generation to generation.

programs.name: Taiko-hajime (opening drum)
programs.text: The first of the 24 plays. The kagura offering begins with this Taiko-hajime.

programs.name: Arashio (purifying the four directions)
programs.text: A dance that purifies the four directions and prays for long life for the local parishioners.

programs.name: Niken (sword dance)
programs.text: The signature play of Hirado Kagura. It is also called 'Sanbon-mai' (three-sword dance) because it uses three real swords. It is the most difficult dance, demanding skill, stamina and concentration. It is even said that how well Niken is danced decides how well the whole kagura goes.

viewing: Daidaikagura, in which all 24 plays are danced (also called Iwato Kagura), is offered only at the autumn annual grand festival of Kameoka Shrine in Hirado (26 October every year). It takes 7-8 hours to finish.
At festivals of other shrines, the number of plays danced matches the rank of the festival. If there is a play you want to see, it is best to check the shrine's information beforehand.
The signature play 'Niken' is a tense dance using real swords. If it is performed, be sure to watch it closely.
